summary: For ages 7–9, build an understanding of the Arctic tundra as a cold, treeless LAND (not sea ice) where permafrost — permanently frozen ground just below the surface — blocks deep roots and drainage. Together with the cold, wind and short summer, this means mostly low plants grow, such as mosses, lichens, tough grasses, small flowers and dwarf shrubs. Teach the CAUSES behind the features (no trees because of frozen ground, cold, wind and a short season), the dramatic winter→summer pulse when the top layer thaws and life bursts out, and a small memorable cast of wildlife (caribou/reindeer, musk oxen, lemmings, snowy owls). Tier A: say it is a cold, treeless land with frozen ground; Tier B: explain why few/no trees grow; Tier C: describe how the short summer lets low plants and animals burst into a brief season of plenty.
misconceptions: The tundra is empty and lifeless — it teems briefly each summer with plants, insects and grazing animals
There are no trees because nothing was planted — permafrost, cold, wind and a short season prevent tree growth
Permafrost is just cold soil — it is ground that stays frozen year-round, blocking drainage and roots
The tundra is the same as the icy sea part of the Arctic — the tundra is land, not floating sea ice
Nothing grows in the tundra at all — low mosses, lichens and tough grasses thrive in the short summer

activities.title: Peel back the ground: finding permafrost
steps: Look at a wide, treeless tundra landscape under a low sun and describe what you notice (no trees, flat, cold-looking).
Open a soil cross-section/cutaway showing a thin 'active layer' of thawed summer soil sitting on top of deep, permanently frozen permafrost.
Explain in your own words why big tree roots can't dig down and why water can't drain away, making boggy summer ground.
Answer the prompt 'Where are the trees?' and say which causes matter: frozen ground, cold, wind and short season.
activities.insight: The tundra is treeless because several causes work together: permafrost (permanently frozen ground) blocks deep roots and drainage, while the cold, the wind and the very short, cool summer limit growth — not simply because 'nothing was planted'.

activities.title: Winter to summer: the brief burst of life
steps: Move a season control from winter to summer and watch the drab, frozen land change as the thin top 'active layer' thaws.
Watch low plants — mosses, lichens and tiny flowers — spring up quickly, and notice animals become active to feed and breed: caribou grazing, a lemming darting, a snowy owl watching.
Tap or point to each animal to learn its name and one thing it does in the tundra (e.g. what it eats).
Say why the tundra is NOT an empty, lifeless desert, describing the short, intense summer growing season.
activities.insight: The tundra is treeless but far from lifeless: the top layer thaws in a short summer while deeper ground stays frozen, letting plants and animals pack a whole season of growth and feeding into a brief window.

activities.title: Explain and check: is the tundra empty?
steps: Respond to a classmate's claim: 'Treeless means it's basically a frozen empty desert — nothing grows and no animals live there.' Say whether you agree and why.
Explain what the ground is like just below the surface (permafrost) and why that stops big trees but lets low plants grow.
Describe what changes when the short summer arrives.
Name at least three tundra animals and say what one of them might eat there.
activities.insight: A full explanation links the frozen ground to why trees can't grow, describes the short summer growing season, and names tundra wildlife — treating the tundra as a distinctive, tough ecosystem rather than a barren desert.

checkQuestion: The Arctic tundra is a huge, treeless landscape. A student says 'treeless means it's basically a frozen empty desert — nothing grows and no animals live there.' Is the tundra really empty and lifeless? Explain what the ground is like just below the surface, and what happens in summer.
checkAnswer: No — the tundra is treeless but far from lifeless. Just below the surface is PERMAFROST — permanently frozen ground — which stops big tree roots growing, so instead low plants like mosses, lichens and tough grasses grow. In the short Arctic SUMMER the top layer thaws and these plants burst into life quickly, and animals such as caribou/reindeer, musk oxen, lemmings and snowy owls live there. So it's a special, tough ecosystem, not an empty desert — the permafrost and short growing season shape what can live and grow.
